says: No recorded session has ever come near the context ceiling: the highest peak is 66,162 tokens, 26.5 percent of the 250,000 limit, and the median is 20,179, 8.1 percent. Zero sessions reached half the ceiling, one reached a quarter and fifteen reached a tenth. Two sessions did cross the compaction target in force when they ran, 66,162 against 63,000 and 57,326 against 50,000, and the two targets differ because the band shares in konst moved between them. Nothing has ever been evicted by the in-place rewrite: zero compaction events on any step of any recorded session. What ran twice instead was the fork, which isolates and continues, matching the two crossings one for one. The re-fetch rate is therefore defined rather than undefined, and it is 0 of 2: neither continuation repeated a pre-fork tool call, and the one time one wanted old material it fetched the artifact handle the carry already held. The condition under which this starts to matter is named: a session several times longer than any recorded, a smaller ceiling, a model with a smaller window, or a task reading much larger results than this corpus of many small calls.

says: The tool schemas a turn sends cost 16,575 bytes on every request, about 4,143 tokens for all 18 tools, and deferring them is not worth building. The figure is measured by encoding a real request with and without the tools array and taking the difference; summing the tools individually gives 16,492, and the 83 byte gap is the array's own brackets and commas. Caching is what decides it: on the measured turn the block was written to cache once on step one and never again across eleven steps, and 81.6 percent of that turn's billed input was cache reads. Across the corpus, 24 recorded turns wrote to cache and 23 of them made a second model call and read the write back; at today's 18 tool scale, 14 of 15 did. The deferral mechanism is named and costed rather than assumed: a catalog line plus a fetch before first use would have added 5 round trips to the measured turn to save at most 2,873 tokens, paid once at cache-write price. The only case it would pay is a turn that makes exactly one model call and never returns, which was 1 of 24.

says: Jev scored 25 of 27 against a regular expression's 24 of 27 on a corpus of real recorded tool results, and a rerun minutes later tied both arms at 24, so the report's conclusion is that the corpus cannot decide this rather than that the judgment won. Both arms score high because this project's recorded sessions carry almost no adversarial instruction-shaped text: what looks like a directive is nearly always the harness's own scaffolding, an oversized-result notice, a bash-timeout caution or a refused-citation notice, never a planted attack. Neither arm's mistakes sit inside the other's: the regular expression's three misses are directive-shaped words inside ordinary Go source or a test assertion rather than text addressed to a reader, and jev's two misses are the same refused-citation caution scored at 0.18, under its own line, which the literal word match caught. The two-task test found no separation, 0.03 to 0.06 apart on three cases, which is the opposite of what the shell sift found. Deciding two arms that both score in the high eighties needs a few hundred labelled cases, and this corpus is 27. It cost $0.000935 over 27 live calls.

says: Running four candidate search patterns over the whole tree costs 320 ms against 14 ms for the literal, so the plan's claim that they cost nothing is false as written and the first implementation spent 638 ms of candidate scan on an 819 ms call. Each form now runs only where it can change the answer: the word boundary and go symbol forms match a subset of the literal, so they are free at 11 ms of a 165 ms call against 131 ms spent reading files. Telling an absence from a wrong pattern is not free, about 590 ms against 150 ms, roughly 3.5x. Over 20 replayed recorded searches, 6 returned nothing and a candidate form rescued 0 of them: not one was a case error. What it buys is the other half, 30 percent of real searches now saying absence rather than being ambiguous. The self answer check caught four leaks across two rounds, including the bench's own test file answering a recorded pattern.
